opus-5.5.text:
I think the main reason is that a biography gives you a whole life, not just a highlight reel. When we read about someone successful, we usually see the final result: the famous paper, the company, the breakthrough. A good biography shows you what came before that: the confusion, the wrong turns, the years when nothing seemed to work, and the decisions that only looked obvious afterward. That's much closer to what your own life feels like from the inside.

The second reason is that it widens your sense of what's possible. When you're young, especially in research, you tend to think there's one standard path: do well in school, get into a good lab, publish papers, and so on. Then you read about people who switched fields in their thirties, or who worked on something unfashionable for ten years before anyone cared, and you realize the space of possible lives is much bigger than the one your environment shows you. That's freeing.

The third reason is about taste and judgment. In AI, I think one of the most important and least teachable skills is choosing the right problem. You can't really learn that from a textbook. But in biographies you can watch how people made those choices: what they paid attention to, what they ignored, how they handled uncertainty. It's like borrowing decades of someone else's experience, compressed into a few hundred pages.

And honestly, part of it is simply that people are interesting. Technology is ultimately built by humans with their own personalities, insecurities, and obsessions. If you only read papers, you miss that whole layer. Reading about people reminds you that the work and the person can't really be separated.

r001.rationale: The response says biographies show what another person’s life felt like from the inside and let readers borrow decades of their experience, clearly describing a vicarious experience of another life.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's because, honestly, most of the useful things I know about how to do research, or how to make decisions in general, didn't come from papers. They came from seeing how specific people actually lived through specific moments.

A paper gives you the result. It's cleaned up, the story is linear, the motivation in the introduction was probably written after the experiments worked. A biography gives you the mess. You see someone who was wrong for five years, or who got lucky, or who made a choice that looked crazy to everyone around them at the time and only makes sense in hindsight. That's the real distribution of how things happen, and I think most people, especially students, have a very distorted picture of it.

There's also a sample-size argument. One life is very long and you only get to live one. If you read thirty autobiographies, you've effectively watched thirty people run the experiment of "how do I spend my time, what do I bet on, when do I quit." You start to notice patterns that you can't see from inside your own life. Like, almost everyone who did something important spent a long period looking unproductive. Almost everyone had a moment where they ignored what their field thought was the right problem. You can't derive that from first principles, you have to see it over and over.

And then the last thing, which is maybe more personal: biographies give you a sense of scale. When you're stuck on some small thing, it's easy to feel like it's the whole world. Reading about someone's entire life compresses time in a way that makes you realize this quarter, or this paper, or this rejection, is a very small fraction. It's calming. It helps you think in decades instead of weeks, and I think a lot of good decisions, in research and otherwise, come from thinking on the right time horizon.

So I'd say: read them not as inspiration, but as data.

r001.rationale: The response describes biographies as letting readers see how specific people lived through moments and as effectively watching many people navigate their lives, clearly conveying vicarious experience.

astra-6.text:
我觉得读自传和传记最大的价值，是你能看到一个人的想法和选择是怎么形成的。我们平时认识一个人，尤其是一个很成功的人，往往只看到他最后的成就，或者他说过的几句话。但把这些放回他的人生经历里，你会发现，他也有很多不确定的时候，也会走弯路，很多选择在当时并没有一个显而易见的答案。

这对我挺有启发的，因为我们自己做选择的时候，也不知道未来会怎么样。读传记不一定是为了模仿谁，而是看看不同的人怎么面对这种不确定性，他们在意什么，又愿意放弃什么。你会意识到，人生可以有很多种走法。

当然，自传也是一个人回过头来对自己的解释，不一定就是事情的全貌。所以我觉得更值得看的，不是从里面总结几条成功秘诀，而是那些具体的经历、矛盾和取舍。那些东西能帮助你更好地理解别人，也理解自己。

r001.rationale: The response says biographies reveal how someone’s choices formed and how they faced uncertainty, but it does not characterize reading them as a way to experience that person’s life vicariously.

sol-6.1.text:
I like biographies because they show you how a life unfolds, rather than presenting a set of conclusions. When you look at someone successful, it’s easy to think they always knew what they were doing. But when you read their story, you see the uncertainty, the failed attempts, and the decisions that only made sense in hindsight.

That gives you perspective on your own situation. You don’t necessarily copy their choices—the circumstances are different—but you get to see more possibilities for how to live and work. And autobiographies are especially interesting because you can see how someone understands their own life, even if that account is selective. I think that’s often more useful than a book telling you directly what you should do.

r001.rationale: It says biographies let readers see how another person’s life unfolds, including uncertainty, failures, and decisions, conveying an indirect experience of that life.
